definition: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that decomposes pretrained weights into magnitude and direction components, then applies LoRA to the direction component for improved learning behavior.
details: DoRA analyzes the difference between full fine-tuning and LoRA and finds that LoRA lacks the negative directional-magnitude correlation seen in full fine-tuning. By learning magnitude separately and using low-rank updates for direction, DoRA improves accuracy and training stability over LoRA. It has been integrated into libraries such as PEFT and can be merged into the base weights.

explainer.lead: DoRA is a fine-tuning method that splits each weight into a size and a direction and trains the direction with LoRA. It matters because it gets closer to full fine-tuning quality at about the same cost as LoRA.

tiers.eli5: Think of every weight as an arrow: it has a length and it points somewhere. DoRA lets you adjust how long each arrow is and nudge where it points, using only a few cheap knobs, instead of rebuilding every arrow.
tiers.practitioner: DoRA keeps the pretrained weight frozen, learns a per-column magnitude vector, and applies a low-rank LoRA update to the normalised direction. Use it as a drop-in LoRA replacement (PEFT supports it); after training the parts merge back into one weight, so inference costs nothing extra, though training is somewhat slower than plain LoRA.
tiers.paperLevel: Liu et al. decompose W into magnitude m and direction V/||V||, finding that LoRA updates magnitude and direction in lockstep, unlike full fine-tuning. Learning m directly while adapting V with a low-rank product decouples the two and improves accuracy and stability over LoRA at a similar number of trainable parameters.

explainer.example: Fine-tuning a 7B model for instruction following with rank-8 DoRA instead of rank-8 LoRA adds only a magnitude vector per layer and is then merged into the base weights for serving.
